# Symmetric truncation, projective energy, and full-rank pyramid menus

This note proves a new ordinary inequality and an exact stationary-menu application. Section 5 pays EVERY balanced stationary menu in every pyramid over a centrally symmetric base, without an orbit hypothesis. It does not reduce an arbitrary convex body to such pyramids, and it does not prove OC.

## 1. A one-dimensional inequality for every even unimodal density

Let phi be a nonnegative, nonzero, integrable even function on the real line, nonincreasing on the positive halfline. For simplicity assume compact support and boundedness, as holds for the convex-body applications below. Write M=int phi. Fix T>0, put

    v=M^(-1) int_{s<=T} phi(s) ds,

and suppose 1/2<v<=1. For every real exponent p>=2, there is a scalar c with 1+cs>0 throughout the captured support such that

    M^(-1) int_{s<=T} (1+cs)^(-p) phi(s) ds
                  <= (2v-1)/v.                         (1)

If v=1, choose c=0. Assume henceforth v<1, and set

    k=1-v in (0,1/2),   c_2=-k/T,   c_p=2c_2/p.       (2)

All these denominators are at least 1-k>0 on s<=T.

By layer cake, phi is a positive mixture of indicators of centered intervals [-r,r]. After normalization by M, it is a probability mixture of the uniform probability laws on those intervals: the layer at height h has weight 2r(h) dh/M. Zero-length layers have zero weight. Boundary values of phi and the intervals have no integral role.

For a layer of radius r, define x=min(T/r,1). Its captured probability is (1+x)/2. Consequently, under the layer probability measure,

    E x = 2v-1.                                        (3)

If r>=T, direct integration gives

    (2r)^(-1) int_{-r}^T (1-ks/T)^(-2) ds
      = I_k(x):=x(1+x)/[2(1-k)(x+k)].                  (4)

If r<T, the whole layer is captured and its integral is

    1/[1-(kr/T)^2] <= 1/(1-k^2) = I_k(1).             (5)

The function I_k is continuous on [0,1] and concave, since

    I_k''(x) = -k/(x+k)^3 < 0.                        (6)

Thus (3)--(6), with Jensen's inequality for the layer probability measure, show that the left side of (1) for p=2 and c=c_2 is at most

    I_k(2v-1) = (2v-1)/v.                             (7)

For the remaining exponents, fix a real a>-2. The function

    p |-> (1+a/p)^(-p),  p>=2,

is nonincreasing. Indeed its logarithmic derivative is

    -log(1+a/p) + (a/p)/(1+a/p) <= 0,

because log(1+t)>=t/(1+t) for every t>-1; this last inequality follows by differentiation, with equality at t=0. Apply this with a=2c_2 s, whose value is greater than -2 on the captured support. Pointwise,

    (1+c_p s)^(-p) <= (1+c_2 s)^(-2).

Integration proves (1) with the explicit choice (2). No minimax exchange or concavity of sampled densities is used.

## 2. Truncating a centrally symmetric convex body

Let D be an m-dimensional centrally symmetric convex body, m>=1, with center zero. Let a be nonzero, T>0, and

    A=D intersect {a.b<=T},   v=|A|/|D|.

The origin lies in the interior of A, so 1/2<v<=1. Define its ordinary projective energy by

    E_A(0)=inf_l int_A (1+l.b)^(-m-1) db,              (8)

where the affine denominator is positive on all of A. The positivity requirement permits the usual attained interior energy minimum; the bounds below do not require invoking its attainment.

Then the exact two-sided bound is

    2v-1 <= E_A(0)/|D| <= (2v-1)/v.                  (9)

For the upper bound, the pushforward density of volume on D under s=a.b is even and nonincreasing on s>=0. In dimension m=1 it is constant on its support. For m>=2, the actual section inclusion and Brunn--Minkowski inequality give this monotonicity: a section between heights -t and t contains a Minkowski combination of their equal-volume sections. Apply Section 1 with p=m+1. The explicitly chosen axial denominator 1+c_p a.b is admissible on A, and its integral bounds the infimum (8) from above.

For the lower bound, the symmetric slab

    B=A intersect (-A)=D intersect {|a.b|<=T}

has volume (2v-1)|D| and centroid zero. Every admissible denominator satisfies

    int_A (1+l.b)^(-m-1) db
      >= int_B (1+l.b)^(-m-1) db >= |B|,

the final inequality being Jensen's inequality on B. Taking the infimum proves the lower bound. If A=D, both bounds equal one.

It follows that

    4/9 <= v/[1+E_A(0)/|D|] <= 1/2.                 (10)

Indeed the lower bound in (10) follows from

    v/[1+E_A(0)/|D|] >= v^2/(3v-1) >= 4/9,

where

    v^2/(3v-1)-4/9 = (3v-2)^2/[9(3v-1)] >=0.

The upper bound follows from the lower estimate in (9). In dimension m=1, D=[-1,1] after rescaling and A=[-1,t], the energy is 4t/(1+t), while |D|=2. Equality in the left side of (10) occurs at t=1/3, equivalently v=2/3. Thus the constant 4/9 is sharp uniformly over m>=1. For a fixed higher dimension m>=2 and a proper cut, the exponent comparison in Section 1 is strict on a positive-measure set, so the lower bound in (10) is strict; no higher-dimensional sharpness assertion is made.

## 3. Actual centroidal sections of a pyramid and the energy identity

Write d=m+1 and let

    K=conv(D times {-1}, {(0,H)}),  H>0,
    B_0=H+1.

Its volume is V_K=B_0|D|/d. Consider the apex-oriented through-zero cap

    H_a={ (X,z): z+a.X>=0 },

with raw normal N_a=(a,1). Its actual section is parameterized by

    b in A:=D intersect {a.b<=1},
    X=H b/(B_0-a.b),  z=-a.X.                        (11)

The graph-coarea Jacobian, with respect to the raw margin z+a.X, is

    H^m B_0/(B_0-a.b)^d.

Put

    C_a= H^(d-1)(K intersect boundary H_a)
                       /(|N_a| V_K),
    p_a=|K intersect H_a|/V_K,
    v=|A|/|D|.

Direct integration along the rays from the apex gives

    C_a=(d H^m/|D|) int_A (B_0-a.b)^(-d) db,
    p_a=(H/d) C_a + (1-v).                           (12)

The second term in p_a is the contribution of the base points a.b>1, whose entire apex rays are captured. It must not be omitted.

Assume the section in (11) has centroid zero. By its displayed Jacobian, this is equivalent to

    int_A b (B_0-a.b)^(-d-1) db = 0.                 (13)

The function l |-> int_A(1+l.b)^(-d)db is convex on its convex domain of positive denominators. Its derivative vanishes at l=-a/B_0 by (13), so this is its global minimizer. Its denominator is at least H/B_0>0 on A. Consequently, if C_0 denotes the normalized raw coarea of the horizontal section,

    C_0=d H^m/B_0^d,
    C_a/C_0=E_A(0)/|D|.                              (14)

This identity retains the actual section and its exact energy parameter. It is not a replacement by an arbitrary projective image.

## 4. A full-rank stationary-menu application

Suppose a finite group G of linear symmetries of D has zero fixed subspace, and that the apex-oriented cap H_a in Section 3 has centroidal section. Orbit it under G. Every orbit cap has the same cap fraction p_a and raw coarea C_a; its raw normals have last coordinate one and their horizontal average is zero. The horizontal section is centered at zero because D is centrally symmetric.

Take the orbit with uniform weights within the orbit and add the reversed horizontal cap {z<=0}. Choose total response weights theta_o,theta_h so that

    theta_o C_a = theta_h C_0,  theta_o+theta_h=1.

This gives exact coarea-weighted normal balance. It is the same balance in unit-normal notation: the section area times the inward unit normal is V_K C_a N_a. Let beta be the response-weighted mean cap fraction of this menu. Since the apex-facing horizontal cap has fraction p_0=(H/B_0)^d, formulas (12)--(14) give

    beta=[C_0 p_a + C_a(1-p_0)]/(C_0+C_a),
    1-beta = v/[1+E_A(0)/|D|].                       (15)

By (10),

    1/2 <= beta <= 5/9,
    4/9 <= 1-beta <= 1/2.                            (16)

Thus this menu and the menu obtained by reversing every cap both have weighted mean at least 4/9, and therefore at least

    Gamma_d=(d/(d+1))^d

for every d>=2. The comparison Gamma_d<=4/9 follows from the standard monotonic decrease of (1+1/d)^(-d), or by differentiating -x log(1+1/x) for x>0.

This can be a genuine full-rank irreducible menu, rather than a sum of rank-two menus: for example, a triangular orbit of oblique directions in a two-dimensional base, together with the opposite horizontal normal, gives four normals of rank three when the three orbit normals have a positive minimal horizontal dependence. The proof does not require irreducibility and permits redundant orbits as well.

The earlier symmetric-base pyramid classification applied to H<=d-1, where nonhorizontal/nonvertical centroidal sections were absent. The energy calculation here applies whenever an actual oblique centroidal section exists, including H>d-1. No decomposition of arbitrary menus into orbit/horizontal menus is asserted or needed for the stronger result below.

## 5. Every balanced stationary menu in a symmetric-base pyramid

**Theorem.** Let d>=2 and let K be the pyramid in Section 3, with ANY centrally symmetric (d-1)-dimensional base D and ANY H>0. Let u_j be finitely many unit inward cap normals. Assume each proper through-zero section E_j=K intersect u_j-perp has centroid zero. Put S_j=H^(d-1)(E_j). For any probabilities theta_j satisfying

    sum_j theta_j S_j u_j=0,

the response-weighted cap mean satisfies

    sum_j theta_j |K intersect {u_j.w>=0}|/V_K >=4/9.  (17)

In particular it is at least Gamma_d. Reversing all caps shows that the same mean is also at most 5/9. There is no rank, orbit, equal-cap-volume, smoothness, or irreducibility assumption. The bound 4/9 is sharp across all d>=2, already for a triangle at its centroid.

Here is a single affine correction proving the entire theorem. Retain

    p_0=(H/(H+1))^d,
    C_0=d H^(d-1)/(H+1)^d,
    c_*=(p_0-4/9)/C_0.                                (18)

For an apex-oriented nonvertical stationary cap, Sections 2--3 give

    e=C_a/C_0=E_A(0)/|D|,
    2v-1<=e<=(2v-1)/v,
    p_a=1-v+p_0 e.

In particular 0<e<=1 and

    1/(2-e)<=v<=(1+e)/2.                              (19)

These two elementary bounds imply

    4/9 <= v-(4/9)e <=5/9.                            (20)

For the lower inequality, use

    1/(2-e)-(4/9)e-4/9
       =(2e-1)^2/[9(2-e)]>=0.

For the upper inequality, use

    (1+e)/2-(4/9)e=1/2+e/18<=5/9.

Combining (18)--(20) gives, for the apex orientation,

    4/9 <= p_a-c_* C_a <=5/9.                        (21)

For the opposite orientation the cap fraction is 1-p_a and the vertical component of its normalized coarea vector is -C_a. Its corrected fraction is 1-(p_a-c_*C_a), so (21) remains true.

Every nonvertical through-zero cap can be placed in exactly one of these two orientations by scaling its normal so that its last coordinate is 1 or -1. The conversion is exact: with raw N_a=(a,1),

    (S_a/V_K) u_a = C_a N_a,

so C_a is the last coordinate of the normalized coarea vector, not the Euclidean section area itself.

A vertical cap has fraction exactly 1/2, because reflection (X,z)->(-X,z) preserves K and exchanges the two cap sides. Its inward normal has last coordinate zero, so its corrected fraction is also 1/2. No classification of which vertical sections are centered is required for this observation.

Thus EVERY stationary cap in the theorem satisfies the same pointwise affine-correction inequality

    |K intersect H_j|/V_K
       -c_* (S_j/V_K)(u_j)_z >=4/9.                 (22)

Multiplying by theta_j and summing cancels the correction by the last coordinate of the assumed full vector balance. This proves (17). It also shows that full horizontal balance is not needed for this particular pyramid inequality; the theorem retains it because that is the actual stationary-menu hypothesis.

For sharpness in d=2, take D=[-1,1] and H=2. The pyramid is a triangle with centroid zero. Its three facet-parallel vertex caps through zero have centered sections, equal response weights and cap fractions 4/9. They give equality in (17). In fixed higher dimensions the theorem is a valid uniform lower bound, without a claim of dimensional sharpness.

The inequality is a proved full-family scalar correction for this geometric class. It supplies no section-preserving reduction of an arbitrary convex body to a pyramid over a centrally symmetric base; that missing reduction must not be assumed in applying the result to the general continuous stationary-section problem or to OC.
